title: Princess Sophia, suffragette
hook: Duleep's daughter Sophia campaigned for women's votes in Britain

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paris, where Duleep Singh died far from Punjab, and your line was for all exiles. Today, one of the children he left behind.

Outside the gates of Hampton Court Palace, near London, a woman in a fine coat holds up a newspaper for sale. It's called The Suffragette. People walking past might know her face. She lives just across the road, in a grace-and-favor house the old Queen herself granted her. She is a goddaughter of Queen Victoria. Her father was the last Maharaja of the Sikh kingdom, the boy who lost a crown. And here she is on the pavement, selling a paper that demands the vote for women.
screen: `A PRINCESS SELLING A NEWSPAPER.` → `A GODDAUGHTER OF THE QUEEN.` → `THE DAUGHTER OF DULEEP SINGH.`

segments.voice: Sophia Duleep Singh grew up English in every outward way: country houses, ponies, dresses, and later a grace-and-favor home at Hampton Court. She could have stayed there quietly, and nobody would have blinked. As her biographer Anita Anand tells it, a journey to India changed her. She saw Punjab, the land her father had ruled, and people living under a government they had no voice in. Back in Britain, women had no vote either. She joined the women fighting for one, the suffragettes, and she didn't do it from the back row. She walked with the women who went to Parliament to demand the vote, on a day when the crowd was met with force. She refused to pay her taxes, saying in effect: no vote, no tax. So officials seized her things, jewelry among them, and sold them at auction, and the fight went on. Guru Nanak, in the Asa di Var, asks why anyone would speak ill of woman, when it is from woman that kings themselves are born. Sophia was raised far from the Gurus' hymns, and nobody can say how much of them she knew. But a daughter of the Sikh royal house stood in the street for women's equal voice, and the old line and the new march sound alike.
screen: `A COMFORTABLE LIFE AT HAMPTON COURT.` · `A JOURNEY TO INDIA CHANGED HER.` · `NO VOTE, NO TAX.` · `FROM WOMAN, KINGS ARE BORN.` · then, large: `THE PRINCESS MARCHED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one cause you think is fair, large or small: a neighbor who isn't being heard, a rule at work that falls hard on some people, a question of who gets a say. Don't argue it out; just hold it, and let one small, peaceful thing you could do for it come to mind, a signature, a phone call, a word in a meeting. If you pray, you can say Waheguru over it.
Princess Sophia. Sophia Duleep Singh, daughter of the last Maharaja, goddaughter of a queen, who marched and refused her taxes for women's right to vote. Today's word.
Your line: the princess marched. A goddaughter of the Queen, out on the pavement. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs in Britain remember Princess Sophia Duleep Singh as a suffragette, and her story is often told alongside the Gurus' teaching that women and men are equal in the sangat.

notes: No dates given in the voice. The march referred to is the deputation of November 1910 ('Black Friday'); confirm Sophia's presence against Anand.
Tax refusal and auction of her jewelry: confirm details; 'she bought some of them back' is told as 'the story goes' and should be checked or cut.
Hampton Court home (Faraday House) as a grace-and-favor residence granted by Queen Victoria: confirm.
Asa di Var, Ang 473 (so kiu manda aakhiai jit jameh rajaan) paraphrased; the script says plainly nobody can say how much gurbani Sophia knew. Confirm the framing is fair.
Original-language game left null: no single Gurmukhi word was certain enough for this day.
Editor: cut the unverified 'she bought some of them back, the story goes' line from the teach.

Audit: Faraday House stands across the road from Hampton Court Palace, not inside the grounds, and was granted to Sophia herself; hook corrected. She moved there as an adult, so the teach now says 'later'. Cut the unsourced claim that the government 'would rather nobody read' The Suffragette.
